table.caption: Height h(t) of a beanbag, in feet, t seconds after it is tossed upward from a hand 6 feet above the ground

model-selection-s2.title: Volume of an open box
model-selection-s2.text: Squares of side $x$ inches are cut from the corners of a $12$-inch by $12$-inch sheet, and the sides are folded up to make an open box. The plot shows the volume $V$, in cubic inches, for six cut sizes.

plot.label: Scatter plot of box volume V in cubic inches against cut size x in inches, rising to about 128 near x = 2 and falling toward 0 near x = 6

items.q: The inputs in the table are equally spaced. Which type of function model fits the data best?
options: Linear, because the outputs rise and then fall by equal amounts
Quadratic, because the second differences are constant
Quadratic, because the first differences are constant
Cubic, because there are five data points

why.correct: Over equal input steps of $0.5$, the first differences are $12, 4, -4, -12$ and the second differences are $-8, -8, -8$. Constant second differences over equal steps mean a quadratic model.
options: A linear model has constant first differences; these change from $12$ to $-12$.
Second differences of $-8$ each time, over equal steps.
The first differences change; it is the second differences that are constant.
Five points do not force a cubic; the pattern of differences decides the type.

items.q: Over the equal input steps of the table, what is the constant second difference of $h$?

mistakes.why: Subtract in order, later minus earlier: $4 - 12 = -8$. The heights rise more slowly, so the change is negative.
That is a first difference. Take the differences of the first differences.

why.correct: First differences: $18 - 6 = 12$, $22 - 18 = 4$, $18 - 22 = -4$, $6 - 18 = -12$. Second differences: $4 - 12 = -8$ each time.

items.q: A quadratic model $h$ fits the table. For which inputs does the context allow the model to be used?
options: Any real number $t$
$0 \le t \le 2$, the inputs in the table
From $t = 0$ until $h$ reaches its maximum at $t = 1$
From $t = 0$ until the time when $h(t) = 0$

why.correct: Time starts at the toss, $t = 0$, and the model stops describing the beanbag when it reaches the ground, where $h(t) = 0$. After that the model gives negative heights, which the context does not allow.
options: Negative times come before the toss, and late times give negative heights.
The beanbag is still in the air at $t = 2$; the model can be used until it lands.
The beanbag keeps falling after its highest point, and the model still describes it.
The toss starts the clock and the ground ends the flight.

items.q: Which statement uses the table to explain why a linear model is not appropriate?
options: The changes over equal steps, $12, 4, -4, -12$, are not constant
Some heights are below $10$ feet, so a linear model would not fit
The inputs go up by $0.5$, not by $1$, so a linear model does not apply
A linear model would need the heights to double each $0.5$ second

why.correct: A linear model has a constant rate of change, so over equal input steps its output changes are equal. Here they are $12, 4, -4, -12$.
options: Equal steps with unequal changes rule out a constant rate.
A line can take small values too; the size of the heights does not decide the type.
A linear model works with any equal step size; the size of the step does not decide the type.
Doubling describes repeated multiplying, not a linear pattern.

items.q: Which type of function model is most appropriate for the box volume $V$ as a function of the cut size $x$?
options: Quadratic, because the data rise and then fall
Cubic, because volume is length times width times height, each depending on $x$
Linear, because the cut size changes by equal steps
Quadratic, because area depends on two lengths

why.correct: The box is $12 - 2x$ by $12 - 2x$ by $x$, so $V(x) = x(12 - 2x)^2$, a product of three linear factors: a cubic. Volume contexts suggest cubic models.
options: Rising then falling fits a cubic here too; the volume context points to degree $3$.
Three dimensions, each linear in $x$, multiply to a cubic.
Equal steps in the input say nothing about the model type by themselves.
Volume uses three lengths, not two.

items.q: What domain does the context allow for the volume model?

why.correct: The cut must have positive size, and two cuts of $x$ must fit along a $12$-inch side: $2x < 12$, so $x < 6$. At $x = 6$ there is no base left.
options: Two cuts come out of each side, so $2x < 12$.
A cut of $7$ inches is impossible on a $12$-inch sheet.
Positive cuts that leave a base.
These are only the cut sizes plotted; any size between $0$ and $6$ makes a box.

items.q: Using $V(x) = x(12 - 2x)^2$, what volume, in cubic inches, does the model predict for a cut of $x = 2$ inches?

mistakes.why: That is $(12 - 2 \cdot 2)^2$, the area of the base; multiply by the height $x = 2$.
That is $2(12 - 2)^2$; the cut is taken from both ends, $12 - 2(2) = 8$.

items.q: Which is an assumption built into the model $V(x) = x(12 - 2x)^2$?
options: The sheet has no thickness, so the folded sides add nothing to the size
The volume increases as the cut size increases
The cuts are whole numbers of inches
The box has a lid

why.correct: The formula uses the full $12 - 2x$ for the inside length, which treats the material as having no thickness. Real cardboard would make the box a little smaller inside.
options: The formula ignores the thickness of the sheet.
The plot shows the volume rising and then falling.
Any cut size between $0$ and $6$ works in the formula.
The box is open; the formula has no lid in it.

items.q: A phone plan costs $\$30$ per month for up to $5$ gigabytes of data, and $\$8$ for each gigabyte over $5$. Which type of model fits the monthly cost?
options: Linear for any usage, at $\$8$ per gigabyte
Piecewise-defined, constant then linear
Quadratic, because the cost rises faster later
Cubic, because the plan has three numbers

why.correct: The cost behaves differently on two intervals: constant at $\$30$ up to $5$ gigabytes, then rising by $\$8$ per gigabyte. Different behavior on different intervals calls for a piecewise-defined model.
options: The cost is flat at first, so one line does not fit.
Two rules, one for each interval of usage.
The rate is constant after $5$ gigabytes; a quadratic's rate would keep changing.
The number of constants does not set the degree.

items.q: For a function on equal input intervals, the average rates of change are $2, 5, 8, 11$. Which model type fits?
options: Linear
Cubic
Quadratic
Piecewise-defined, with two constant pieces

why.correct: The average rates of change increase by $3$ each time: the rate of change changes at a constant rate. That is the pattern of a quadratic.
options: A linear function has the same rate on every interval.
A cubic's rates change by changing amounts.
A rate of change that changes linearly gives a quadratic.
Constant pieces would have rates of $0$.

items.q: Which contexts suggest a quadratic model? Select all that apply.
options: The area of a square patio as a function of its side length
The height of a ball thrown upward as a function of time
The total price of tickets at $\$12$ each as a function of the number bought
The volume of a cube as a function of its edge length

why.correct: Area depends on two lengths and gives degree $2$; the height of a thrown object has a rate of change that falls at a constant rate. A constant price gives a linear model; volume gives a cubic.
options: Side times side: degree $2$.
The height rises, peaks once and falls symmetrically.
Each ticket adds $\$12$: a constant rate, so linear.
Edge cubed: degree $3$.

items.q: A linear model $T(m) = 90 - 4m$ gives the temperature, in degrees Celsius, of soup $m$ minutes after it is set on a counter in a $22$-degree room. Which restriction on the domain does the context suggest?
options: $0 \le m \le 17$, because after that the model gives temperatures below the room's
$0 \le m \le 22.5$, because $T$ is $0$ at $m = 22.5$
$m \ge 0$, because time is not negative
$0 \le m \le 90$, because the soup starts at $90$ degrees

why.correct: Soup cools toward room temperature and does not go below it. $90 - 4m = 22$ at $m = 17$, so the model is reasonable only for $0 \le m \le 17$.
options: The soup never cools to $0$ degrees in a $22$-degree room.
The upper end matters too: the model drops below room temperature.
The starting temperature is an output, not a bound on time.

items.q: A garage models its fee as $F(h) = 12 + 0.75h$ dollars for $h$ hours, and the model applies for $0 \le h \le 24$. What is the greatest fee the model allows, in dollars?

mistakes.why: That is the least fee, at $h = 0$; the fee rises with time.
That is the hourly part, $0.75 \cdot 24$; add the $\$12$ base fee.

why.correct: $F$ is increasing, so its greatest value on $[0, 24]$ is at $h = 24$: $F(24) = 12 + 0.75(24) = 30$ dollars. The restricted domain restricts the range to $[12, 30]$.

items.q: Through any five points with different inputs there is a polynomial of degree at most $4$. Why might a student still not choose it to model five data points?
options: It misses one or more of the five data points it was built from
Polynomials of degree $4$ have no real zeros
It may turn in ways the context gives no reason for
It has a constant rate of change

why.correct: Such a polynomial matches the data exactly, but between and beyond the points it may wiggle, with turning points the situation does not support. A simpler model that matches the pattern of the data and the context is usually more useful.
options: It does pass through all five; that is how it is chosen.
Many degree-$4$ polynomials have real zeros.
Matching the points is not the same as matching the situation.
Only linear functions have a constant rate.

items.q: Output values over equal input steps are $3, 7, 11, 15, 19$. Which model type fits and why?
options: Quadratic, because the outputs increase
Linear, because the outputs are odd numbers
Quadratic, because the second differences are $4$
Linear, because the first differences are all $4$

why.correct: Over equal input steps the outputs change by $4$ each time: constant first differences mean a constant rate of change, so a linear model fits.
options: Increasing outputs fit many models; the differences decide.
Whether the outputs are odd is not a property of the model.
The second differences are $0$; the first differences are $4$.
Equal steps, equal changes.

items.q: Over equal input steps, a data set has outputs $1, 8, 27, 64, 125$. The first differences are $7, 19, 37, 61$, the second differences are $12, 18, 24$, and the third differences are $6, 6$. Which model type fits?
options: Linear, because the outputs rise at each step
Quadratic, because the second differences are constant
Cubic, because the third differences are constant
Quartic, because there are five data points

why.correct: Over equal input steps, a polynomial of degree $n$ has constant $n$th differences. Here the first and second differences change and the third differences are constant, $6$, so a cubic model fits.
options: A linear model needs constant first differences. These are $7, 19, 37, 61$.
The second differences are $12, 18, 24$, which are not constant.
The third differences, $6$ and $6$, are the first ones that are constant.
Five points can be matched by a quartic, but the constant third differences show that a simpler cubic already fits.
